title: Distributed-HISQ: A Distributed Quantum Control Architecture
problem: Distributed quantum control architectures (DQCAs) for superconducting qubits face two blockers: existing lock-step synchronization schemes incur large execution overheads (idle time or full program broadcast across controllers), and existing quantum ISAs are either too high-level or too hardware-specific to support diverse qubit technologies and gate implementation strategies on a single microarchitecture.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires thousands to millions of qubits, making distributed control inevitable, yet nondeterministic feedback loop latencies demand cycle-accurate cross-controller synchronization that current lock-step and demand-driven schemes cannot provide efficiently.
method: Distributed-HISQ combines two mechanisms. HISQ is a hardware instruction set extending RISC-V 32I that represents quantum operations as timed commands: 'send codeword X to port Y at time T'—this separation lets the same instructions work across different quantum hardware and electronics implementations. BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol) eliminates synchronization overhead by letting controllers reserve their sync points in advance instead of requesting sync on demand; since quantum gates run for a fixed, known duration, the system can send synchronization messages during this execution time, achieving zero-cycle overhead when the preceding operations are long enough to hide communication delays. The system connects controllers using a hybrid tree-and-mesh network topology: a balanced tree handles region-level synchronization, while mesh-like links mirroring the physical qubit layout handle nearest-neighbor synchronization, with only 13 LUTs per SyncU hardware cost on an FPGA.
key_novelty: BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol) lets controllers pre-announce their synchronization points in advance, hiding the communication delay under the fixed-duration execution of preceding quantum gates and enabling zero-cycle synchronization overhead in the common case.
contributions: HISQ: a hardware-agnostic quantum ISA extension to RISC-V that decouples control from quantum semantics and analog implementation, enabling a single microarchitecture to serve multiple qubit technologies
BISP: a booking-based synchronization protocol achieving potentially zero-cycle overhead, implemented in 13 LUTs, supporting both nearest-neighbor and region-level remote synchronization
Full implementation and validation on a commercial 66-qubit superconducting quantum control system (DQCtrl), including qubit-level calibration experiments
Simulation results showing 22.8% average program execution time reduction and ~5x infidelity reduction versus lock-step baseline across dynamic circuit benchmarks

metrics.speedup: 22.8% reduction in average program execution time vs. lock-step baseline
metrics.accuracy: ~5x reduction in infidelity vs. lock-step baseline for long-range CNOT circuits
metrics.other: BISP SyncU costs only 13 LUTs; HISQ full control board: 4155 LUTs, 6392 FFs, 2.46 Mb BRAM

limitations: Region-level synchronization was not achievable in the physical hardware prototype due to limited LVDS connectivity; scalability analysis assumes idealized constant communication latency for the baseline, potentially underestimating baseline overhead.
primary_theme: distributed quantum control architecture with zero-overhead synchronization
